newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rights groups in legal strike at mortgage bias.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rights groups in legal strike at mortgage bias.

text.p: Two civil rights organisations on Thursday launched a first legal strike against what they said was a nationwide pattern of racial discrimination in home mortgage lending.

The American Civil Liberties Union and the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People said they had filed a complaint with the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission alleging a subsidiary of finance company PHH Corp. discriminated against blacks in the Philadelphia area.

"Owning a home is part of the American dream. Unfortunately ... all too often African-Americans have been prevented from participating in that dream because mortgage companies discriminate," Stefan Presser, legal director of Philadelphia ACLU office, told a news conference.

Filing of the state complaint automatically triggers a federal investigation as well, Presser said. Officials of both organisations said the complaint was just the first action in a national legal campaign.

"We hope it represents the first of several filings, both in the Philadelphia area and nationally," said Chris Hansen, a senior attorney with the ACLU national office. "I don't think there's any question that there's a national problem."

The case against PHH was based on data lenders are required to submit under a 1990 federal law aimed at fighting lending discrimination. Such data will also be used to back up the later discrimination cases to be filed by the organisations.
PHH said the company's policy was not to discriminate in its lending practices.

"PHH has a longstanding policy of not discriminating in the process of granting mortgages ... Therefore we were surprised to learn of the actions taken by the ACLU and the NAACP today," it said in a statement.

"PHH was not aware of any issues related to the allegations pertaining to charges of discriminatory mortgage practices. We have no record of any complaint by any mortgage applicant, the ACLU or the NAACP alleging race discrimination in the Philadelphia area."

The company said it had previously aligned with the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. (Freddie Mac) and a Baptist-church owned company to promote home ownership among African-Americans. It said it had not reviewed the ACLU complaint.

An official of the Mortgage Bankers Association, representing lenders, said the ACLU case appeared based on flawed analysis and did not take into account issues such as property values or credit histories of borrowers.
"It's not their (PHH's) fault that statistically, blacks tend to be less creditworthy than the U.S. as a whole," said Paul Mondor, director of regulatory compliance for the association.

The complaint said an analysis of the lending data for 1994 and 1995 demonstrated that PHH rarely lent in black neighbourhoods and that it denied loans to African-Americans in far greater proportion than it did to whites.

In 1994, 5 percent of all whites seeking loans from the company were denied, compared with 18 percent of all blacks who applied for loans. In 1995, 3.7 percent of whites and 6.7 percent of blacks were denied, the ACLU said.
In all, PHH received 1,874 loan applications in the Philadelphia area in 1994, and 1,255 in 1995.
Similar discrimination patterns were found for the period from 1990 through 1993, the group said.
"No factor other than race explained the disparity in the lending practices of PHH," Hansen said.

The discrimination persisted regardless of factors such as income, whether the loan was for a new mortgage or refinancing, or whether it was covered by federal insurance, the complaint said. However, it noted all six low- or moderate-income blacks who applied in 1994 received mortgages and all 25 who applied in 1995 did also.

ACLU spokeswoman Emily Whitfield said it was not clear why the low-to-moderate income blacks received mortgages, but said the absolute number was unacceptably low and bolstered the second charge, that loans were not made in African-American neighbourhoods.

The complaint also said PHH had a far lower market share in black neighbourhoods than it did in white areas. The company markets mortgages over the telephone, and Presser said the disparity could be because the company discriminated in marketing through selected organisations.
